WE also advertises special access arrangements for certain educational and government websites. Examples include:

- https://digital.gov.eg
- https://mcit.gov.eg
- https://tra.gov.eg

issues.title: dokodemo-door with tproxy accepts UDP and logs "tunneling request", but UDP never egresses on the VLESS+XHTTP peer (TCP via same inbound works)
issues.body:
# Draft: issue в XTLS/Xray-core — tproxy-вход роняет UDP (принимается, туннелируется, не выходит)

## Title

dokodemo-door with tproxy accepts UDP and logs "tunneling request", but UDP never egresses on the VLESS+XHTTP peer (TCP via same inbound works)

## Environment

- Xray-core: 26.11.9 (also reproduced on 26.10.31)
- Server A (RU node): inbound `dokodemo-door` with `followRedirect: true`, `sockopt.tproxy: "tproxy"`, nftables TPROXY (`meta l4proto udp tproxy to :12345 meta mark set 1` + `ip rule fwmark 1 lookup 100`), outbound `vless` + `xhttp` (mode `stream-one`) + `reality` to Server B.
- Server B (EU node): inbound `vless` + `xhttp` + `reality`, outbound `freedom`.
- Clients reach Server A via WireGuard tunnel (AWG); UDP and TCP both hit the same TPROXY rule.

## Symptom

- TCP through the same tproxy inbound → egresses on Server B fine (full internet via B's IP).
- UDP: packet arrives at Server A (tcpdump on WG ingress), xray log shows the correct original destination and `tunneling request to udp:... via <B>:443`, but **nothing egresses on Server B** (tcpdump on egress interface: 0 packets).
- Browser QUIC from clients silently falls back to TCP — the breakage was invisible until a UDP-only application (Xbox Teredo) failed.

## Isolation experiment

Same Server A host, second xray instance, **identical outbound** (vless+xhttp stream-one+reality to B), inbound changed to plain `dokodemo-door` (fixed `address`/`port`, **no tproxy**) on 127.0.0.1. UDP sent to it **egresses on Server B correctly**. So the transit path and version are fine; the tproxy ingress path drops UDP.

Also tried `xhttpSettings.mode: "auto"` for the outbound — log shows xray still dials `mode stream-one` for UDP; same behavior.

## Minimal repro sketch

Server A:
```json
{
  "inbounds": [{
    "port": 12345, "protocol": "dokodemo-door",
    "settings": { "network": "tcp,udp", "followRedirect": true },
    "streamSettings": { "sockopt": { "tproxy": "tproxy" } }
  }],
  "outbounds": [{
    "protocol": "vless",
    "settings": { "vnext": [{ "address": "<B>", "port": 443, "users": [{ "id": "<uuid>", "encryption": "none" }] }] },
    "streamSettings": {
      "network": "xhttp", "security": "reality",
      "realitySettings": { "serverName": "<sni>", "publicKey": "<key>", "shortId": "<id>" },
      "xhttpSettings": { "mode": "stream-one" }
    }
  }]
}
```
nftables on A: `... udp dport <test> tproxy to :12345 meta mark set 1` (+ `ip rule fwmark 1 lookup 100` → `local default dev lo`... note: our table 100 is `default dev lo` for tproxy delivery — standard setup).

Send any UDP datagram into the TPROXY rule → observe: accepted (log), tunneled (log), zero egress on B.

## Ask

Is UDP via dokodemo-tproxy ingress expected to work in 26.x? If yes — this looks like a regression/bug in the tproxy UDP path (or its interaction with XHTTP UDP carrying); happy to collect any specific diagnostics (pcap, debug logs).

## Notes

- Possibly related area: PR #7386 (fake UDP sockets in TPROXY mode) — symptom there was resource leak, not silent drop.
- Our workaround (separate non-xray UDP tunnel) is in place; reporting upstream so the tproxy path can be fixed for everyone.

issues.title: HTTPUpgrade client: Close the connection when the upgrade fails
issues.body:
When the upgrade request could not be sent, or the server did not answer with a valid "101 Switching Protocols", the dial returned the error and left the TCP connection open until the garbage collector closed it.

With "fingerprint": "unsafe", a failed TLS handshake is one of these cases. Go's TLS does the handshake at the first write, and here the first write is the upgrade request.

issues.title: Happy Eyeballs: add successDefinition to race until TLS handshake completes
issues.body:
## Motivation

When the server's domain resolves to several IPs, Happy Eyeballs is supposed to pick a working one. In Russia, however, some ISPs (the DPI boxes installed at them) drop the ServerHello for some of these IPs while TCP to them still connects. Which IPs are affected differs from one ISP and region to another and changes over time: an IP that is blocked for one client works for another, so removing it from DNS would only break it for everyone else. Happy Eyeballs today ends the race at the first TCP connection, so it happily picks such an IP, and then the TLS or REALITY handshake can never complete. A retry usually picks the same IP again, because it wins the TCP race again. In this situation the current Happy Eyeballs is of no use at all, even though other IPs of the same domain work fine.

## What this PR adds

A new optional field `successDefinition` in `sockopt.happyEyeballs`:

| Value | The race is won by |
|---|---|
| `tcpConnected` (default) | the first established TCP connection, as before |
| `tlsHandshakeComplete` | the first connection that completes the TLS or REALITY handshake |

```json
"sockopt": {
  "domainStrategy": "UseIP",
  "happyEyeballs": {
    "tryDelayMs": 250,
    "maxConcurrentTry": 4,
    "successDefinition": "tlsHandshakeComplete"
  }
}
```

Without `successDefinition`, or with `tcpConnected`, nothing changes. Without TLS or REALITY, `tlsHandshakeComplete` is the same as `tcpConnected`.

The behaviour follows section 6.1 of Happy Eyeballs v3, which says clients SHOULD wait for the TLS handshake to complete before canceling other attempts: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-happy-happyeyeballs-v3/
Chromium's Happy Eyeballs v3 implementation does the same: a TCP-based attempt runs the TLS handshake inside it and completes only when the handshake does, and an attempt counts as slow (so the next one starts) if TCP and TLS together take longer than the connection attempt delay:
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/socket/tls_stream_attempt.cc
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/http/http_stream_pool_attempt.cc

Happy Eyeballs v3 is still a draft, and browsers do not use it by default yet: in Chromium it is behind the `HappyEyeballsV3` feature, which is disabled by default, and Firefox enables it only in Nightly.

## How it works

- The scheduler of `TcpRaceDial` is reused as is (`tryDelayMs`, `maxConcurrentTry`, `prioritizeIPv6`, `interleave`); only the attempt it runs differs. With `tcpConnected` the attempt is the same system dial as before.
- With `tlsHandshakeComplete` every attempt goes through TCP dial to one IP → FinalMask (if any) → the transport's own TLS or REALITY handshake. Only the TCP destination changes from attempt to attempt; masks apply to each attempt separately, exactly as on a normal dial.
- An attempt keeps its `maxConcurrentTry` slot until its handshake ends, and a hanging handshake does not stop the scheduler from starting the next attempt after `tryDelayMs`.
- Losing attempts are stopped by closing their connections. Transports that leave the handshake to the first write (gRPC, and HTTPUpgrade and XHTTP with Go TLS) get it completed inside the race, so a connection is never handshaked twice.
- The race happens under the same conditions as the TCP race in `DialSystem`: `domainStrategy` set, at least two IPs, no `dialerProxy`, non-zero `tryDelayMs` and `maxConcurrentTry`. Otherwise the transport dials exactly as before.

All covered transports now dial through `internet.DialTCPWithHandshake(ctx, dest, streamSettings, handshake)`. `handshake` is a function that wraps the TCP connection with the transport's TLS or REALITY client; it holds the same code the transport used to run right after its own TCP dial.

Transports covered: RAW (TLS, REALITY), WebSocket, HTTPUpgrade, gRPC (TLS, REALITY), XHTTP over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (TLS, REALITY), MASQUE over HTTP/2. For XHTTP the race runs once per new physical connection. UDP

issues.title: [Feature] XMC: Yggdrasil third-party login + texture signature verification / XMC 支持 Yggdrasil 第三方登录与材质签名验证
issues.body:
> Status: proposal / ready for discussion. Branch: `feat/xmc-yggdrasil-login` (based on `c4561418`), commits `109e8d2c` + `74eb4feb`.
> 状态：提案，欢迎讨论。分支：`feat/xmc-yggdrasil-login`（基于 `c4561418`），提交 `109e8d2c` + `74eb4feb`。

---

## 中文

### 背景与动机

当前 XMC 的登录认证是自造的：

- 客户端配置里手工填写 `username` / `uuid` / `texturesValue` / `texturesSignature`（需要自己去 Mojang 或皮肤站查 UUID、拉签名材质再复制进配置）；
- 服务端用预共享 `password`（同时作为 RSA 私钥的派生种子）加静态 `profiles` 白名单校验；
- Verify Token 尾部追加预共享密码，和 Minecraft 协议本身没有关系。

维护成本高，且无法复用 Minecraft 生态已有的标准在线模式认证（Yggdrasil / authlib-injector / Blessing Skin）。更重要的是，**如果后续要给 MC 模组实现 XMC 服务端**（让真实 MC 客户端或服务端模组走标准 Yggdrasil 登录接入 XMC），预共享密码模型无法对接，因为模组侧只会实现标准的 `authenticate` / `join` / `hasJoined` 流程。

本次改动把 XMC 改成标准 Yggdrasil 登录客户端 + 标准 `hasJoined` 服务端校验，并补上材质签名验证，为后续 MC 模组实现 XMC 服务端铺路，也为 XMC 客户端将来接入真实 MC 服务端打基础。

### 修改内容

涉及文件：

- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/yggdrasil.go`（新增：Yggdrasil HTTP 客户端、登录/刷新/join/hasJoined、验签）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/client.go`（Yggdrasil 登录、标准 hash、材质验签接入）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/server.go`（hasJoined 校验、随机密钥、断连语义）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/profile.go`（多 properties 读写、身份/材质比较）
- `transport/internet/finalmask/xmc/config.go`、`config.proto`、`config.pb.go`
- `infra/conf/transport_finalmask.go`（`yggdrasil` 配置解析、随机密钥生成、警告输出）
- 测试：`yggdrasil_test.go`、`profile_test.go`、`handshake_test.go`、`infra/conf/transport_finalmask_xmc_test.go`

#### 1. 配置

XMC `settings` 新增可选的 `yggdrasil` 段：

```json
{
  "type": "xmc",
  "settings": {
    "hostname": "mc.example.com",
    "yggdrasil": {
      "api": "https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil",
      "username": "user@example.com",
      "password": "<skin account password>",
      "player": "Steve"
    }
  }
}
```

- `api`：Yggdrasil API root（例如 Blessing Skin 的 `/api/yggdrasil`）；
- `username` / `password`：客户端登录凭据（邮箱或角色名，取决于 API 实现）；
- `player`：可选；账号有多个角色时必须指定；
- 服务端只需要 `api`，不需要账号密码。

Yggdrasil 模式下顶层 `password` 不再参与握手和密钥派生；旧配置（无 `yggdrasil` 段）行为完全不变。

#### 2. 客户端（client.go / yggdrasil.go）

- 通过 `authserver/authenticate` 登录，多角色时用 `authserver/refresh` 携带 `selectedProfile` 绑定 token；token/clientToken 进程内缓存，`/join` 遇到 403 自动重新登录重试一次。
- Login Start 使用皮肤站返回的真实角色名和 UUID。
- 加密协商完成后按原版算法计算 login hash：

  `sha1(serverId + sharedSecret + serverPublicKey)`，并按 Java `BigInteger#toString(16)` 的二进制补码规则渲染（包含负号和去前导零）。

- **使用 Encryption Request 中实际收到的公钥计算哈希，不再固定配置公钥**；Yggdrasil 模式客户端不需要也不应该去“确认公钥”。
- 用 `accessToken` 真实调用 `sessionserver/session/minecraft/join`。
- 解析 Login Success 的多个 properties，并用 API root 中的 `signaturePublickey` 校验 `textures` 属性签名：
  - SHA1withRSA（与 Blessing Skin 的 `openssl_sign` 默认算法、Minecraft 客户端的签名校验一致）；
  - 支持 PEM / 裸 base64 公钥；
  - 公钥按账号缓存，验签失败时自动重新拉取一次（覆盖皮肤站轮换密钥）；
  - `textures` 缺失、无签名、签名不匹配都会拒绝登录；
  - 校验发生在发送 Login Acknowledged 之前，失败不会进入 play 阶段。
- Yggdrasil 模式不再往 Verify Token 尾部追加预共享密码，保持和原版客户端一致的报文形状。

#### 3. 服务端（server.go）

- Yggdrasil 模式下每个进程随机生成 1024-bit RSA 密钥对（与原版服务端行为一致），**不再从 password 派生**；
- 解密共享密钥后，用自己实际持有的公钥计算同一个 login hash，真实调用 `sessionserver/session/minecraft/hasJoined`；
- 因为客户端 `/join` 与服务端 `/hasJoined` 存在天然竞态，服务端以 200ms 间隔轮询，最长 10s；
- 校验返回的角色 UUID / 名称必须与 Login Start 一致；
- Login Success 直接使用 `hasJoined` 返回的已签名 properties（含 `textures`、`uploadableTextures`）；
- 失败时按原版语义断连：未加入 → `multiplayer.disconnect.unverified_username`，API 异常 → `multiplayer.disconnect.authservers_down`；
- 未配置 `yggdrasil` 时保留原预共享密码 + `profiles` 白名单逻辑。

#### 4. 安全模型与警告

Yggdrasil 模式的安全绑定发生在 Yggdrasil 查询里：中间人两侧分别握手时，客户端提交的 hash 和服务端查询的 hash 必然不同，`hasJoined` 返回空，连接失败；即使不固定服务端公钥也无法完成中间人。

由于这时不再使用预共享密码、也不做密码派生，控制台会在 config 加载时输出一次警告（`errors.LogWarning`）：

```text
XMC: Yggdrasil mode is enabled. The RSA key pair is generated randomly and "password"
is no longer used to derive it or to authenticate the transport; players are verified
through https://skin.example.com/api/yggdrasil (client /join, server /hasJoined).
Both ends must be able to reach the Yggdrasil API. The configured "password" is ignored.
```

### 兼容性

- 不配置 `yggdrasil`：完全保持旧行为（密码派生密钥 + verify to

issues.title: DNS outbound: End UDP sessions once their queries are answered
issues.body:
A UDP session of the DNS outbound never reads EOF, so it lasts until the inbound drops it or its idle timer fires. The timer looks for activity once per connIdle, so a session answered right away ends after two periods, ten minutes by default. The dokodemo-door inbound drops idle UDP after two to three minutes; the TUN inbound never does. Stub resolvers and dnsmasq usually send each query from a new source port, so every query holds a session with three goroutines that long.

On my test bench (linux/arm64, FakeDNS, 5000 queries at 50 per second, a new port per query) RSS grew from 40 MB to 187 MB through dokodemo-door and to 180 MB through TUN, where the goroutines were gone only ten minutes after the last query.

I track the queries a UDP session still owes an answer, hijacked or sent upstream, by ID and question, so a repeated answer settles nothing. While any is open the session keeps connIdle, so a slow lookup is not cut; one second after the last answer it ends, which still leaves room for AAAA sent after A from the same socket. TCP, the session of Xray's own DNS client, a session with more than 256 open queries and a connIdle below one second work as before.

With this change the same load ends at 62 MB through dokodemo-door and 64 MB through TUN. TestUDPDNSSessionsEnd sends 200 A and MX queries, MX forwarded upstream, each from its own socket: on main they leave 600 goroutines behind; with this change they are gone a second after the last answer.

### Description

> 简述：在 v26.10.17（与 main 相同）中，如果 XDRIVE 客户端在下载中途消失（进程被杀或断网），服务端无法察觉：它会继续从目标读取，并把剩余的整个响应写入存储（复现中 20 秒内写入约 235 MiB、607 个对象）。这些对象要等服务端的 mux 子连接自行结束后才会被清理（约 2.7–13 分钟），期间该会话仍被持续 LIST 轮询。原因是 XDRIVE 既没有对端存活检测，也没有背压。

Version: v26.10.17 (`92ccc93`, the newest release and the same commit as current `main`), `network: "xdrive"`, `service: "local"`. XDRIVE is only in the pre-releases since v26.9.30; it is not in v26.3.27. The session logic involved does not depend on the backend, so remote backends behave the same way.

When an XDRIVE client disappears in the middle of a download (process killed, network lost, which is common for mobile clients), the server does not notice:

1. It keeps reading from the target and writes the whole remaining response into the storage. In the repro the client had received 22 MiB of a 256 MiB body; within 20 s after the client was killed the server wrote 246,869,084 bytes in 607 objects.
2. These objects stay until the server-side mux sub-connection ends on its own: about 2.7 min when the target closes the connection after the body, about 13 min with a keep-alive target. Meanwhile the dead session is still polled (about 2 LIST per second).
3. The server logs nothing after the client is gone, even at `debug`.

With a remote backend every abandoned download can upload hundreds of MiB into the storage account, consume API quota and leave the objects there for minutes.

If only the application connection is closed while the client stays alive (curl killed), the server stops writing within about 5 s and the folder is cleaned up, so the problem is specific to the peer disappearing.

| 256 MiB body at 16 MiB/s, `sessionTtlSeconds: 30` | storage at +30 s | +90 s | +180 s | server kept writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| download completes (control) | 0 B | 0 B | 0 B | no |
| client `kill -9` after ~2 s | 246,869,084 B / 607 objects | same | same | yes, the whole remaining body |
| client `SIGTERM` after ~2 s | 246,394,446 B / 515 objects | same | same | yes |
| curl killed, client alive | 0 B (one `.end`) | 0 B | 0 B | no, stopped within ~5 s |
| client `kill -9`, keep-alive target, watched 900 s | 246,453,796 B | same | same | yes; empty only at ~750–780 s |
| client `kill -9`, target sends `Connection: close` | 246,485,923 B | same | 0 B | yes; empty at ~165 s |

- `Listener.claim` marks the session active (`transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go:225`); the mark is removed only in the connection's `onClose` (`xdrive.go:234`). `collect()` skips active sessions (`xdrive.go:267-269`), so the folder of a dead session is not collected while the server-side connection is open.
- That connection is closed only when the inbound handler returns (`app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:123-127`), i.e. after the server-side mux session ends. issues.title: Fix noise after udphop
issues.body:
Fix noise emission when `noise` and `udphop` are used together.

Previously, noise state was keyed by the destination passed to `WriteTo`. udphop could replace that destination internally or switch the source socket without invalidating the noise state. Continuous outgoing traffic also refreshed the noise reset timeout, allowing repeated hops without another noise sequence.

**Implementation**

- Add shared `UDPPath` state through the existing finalmask dialer, containing the actual destination, a generation counter, and a mutex.
- Increment the generation after a successful hop changes the local endpoint, destination IP, or destination port.
- Have the noise wrapper clear its cached reset state when it observes a new generation. The next write emits noise before its payload, then resumes the existing reset behavior.
- Serialize the complete masked write against hopping, keeping all noise packets, configured delays, and the associated payload on the same socket and destination.

```

```

The TUN settings contain no IPv6 at all: `gateway` and `autoSystemRoutingTable` are IPv4-only, `dns` is IPv4-only. The same machine and the same config start fine with a locally patched v26.10.31 that skips the IPv6 `SetDNS` call when the config does not ask for IPv6, so the fatal step is exactly the IPv6 DNS setup.

Why v26.11.9 fails, from the code:

- `Start()` calls `t.luid.SetDNS(family, dns, nil)` for both `AF_INET` and `AF_INET6` (proxy/tun/tun_windows.go:234), regardless of what the config asks for.

- `ipv6Off()` only accepts bit `0x10` (proxy/tun/tun_windows.go:105-113):

  return err == nil && value&0x10 != 0
  ```

issues.title: Tunnel inbound: Close idle fake UDP sockets in TPROXY mode
issues.body:
Fixes #5263 (closed as not planned).

### Problem

With `tproxy` on a Tunnel (dokodemo-door) inbound, replies go through `PacketWriter`. It opens a fake UDP socket bound to each remote address that sends a reply ([dokodemo.go:231-245](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L231-L245)). The sockets are closed only in `Close()` ([:266-273](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L266-L273)), when the UDP session ends ([:189](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L189)).

A cone session ends after its client port has been silent for 2 minutes ([worker.go:397](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go#L397)). Only client packets count as activity ([worker.go:200](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go#L200)). A P2P application sends from one port to many peers and is never silent for 2 minutes. Its session keeps one fake socket for every peer that ever replied.

On a router with transparent proxy (TPROXY → dokodemo-door) xray grew by about 1450 sockets and 7 MB of RSS per hour: 6524 open fds 4.5 hours after a restart that followed an OOM kill. #5263 shows the same growth.

### Reproduction

`05-xray-fakeudp-repro.sh` (below) runs as a normal user in network namespaces: `unshare -Urn sh 05-xray-fakeudp-repro.sh ./xray 10 300`. The client sends from one UDP port to 10 new peers per second. Every 10th datagram goes to a peer first contacted more than 180 s ago. Peers echo from the address they were sent to. Inbound:

```json
{"listen": "0.0.0.0", "port": 1100, "protocol": "tunnel",
 "settings": {"allowedNetwork": "udp", "followRedirect": true},
 "streamSettings": {"sockopt": {"tproxy": "tproxy"}}}
```

```sh
iptables -t mangle -A PREROUTING -i <client-if> -p udp -j TPROXY --on-port 1100 --tproxy-mark 1
ip rule add fwmark 1 lookup 100
ip route add local 0.0.0.0/0 dev lo table 100
```

### Results

`main` at c456141, linux/amd64, 10 new peers/s, open fds of the xray process:

| time, s | main | with this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 60 | 609 | 609 |
| 120 | 1209 | 1209 |
| 180 | 1809 | 1508 |
| 240 | 2349 | 1501 |
| 300 | 2888 | 1495 |

Both builds: 3000/3000 replies, 120/120 replies from old peers, none from a wrong address.

Router, arm64, v26.7.28 with the same change: 6524 fds and growing before; about 880 without a trend 15 hours later, 575 five days later.

### Change

- `PacketWriter` records when each remote last sent a reply.
- `WriteMultiBuffer`, at most every 30 s, closes and forgets the fake sockets of remotes silent for 2 minutes. The next reply from such a remote opens a new socket through the existing path.
- The socket of the original destination (`w.conn`) is never closed early. Datagrams without a `UDP` address are written to it too ([:255](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L255)). Before, one write error on it closed it for the rest of the session.
- On a write error the map entry is deleted instead of set to `nil`.

The sweep runs on the writer goroutine: no new goroutine, no lock. 2 minutes matches the session timeout in `worker.go`. If replies stop completely, the sweep waits for the next write, which is the old behavior.

### Tests

- `TestSweepIdleClosesOnlyIdleFakeSockets` in `proxy/dokodemo/fakeudp_sweep_test.go`.

issues.body:
### Problem

`mustSendRecvTcp` in `transport/internet/finalmask/tcp_test.go` calls `t.Fatal` from the writer goroutine, which `go vet` flags:

```
tcp_test.go:30: call to (*T).Fatal from a non-test goroutine
```

`t.Fatal` ends that goroutine via `runtime.Goexit`, so `close(waitCh)` never runs and the helper's final `<-waitCh` blocks until the package test timeout, losing the write error with it. Send the error over `waitCh`, which is already declared `chan error`, and check it on the test goroutine. The channel is buffered so the writer still cannot block, matching the previous `close`. This is the pattern already used by `TestTCPcustomClientRejectsMismatchedServerSequence` and `TestTCPWrapListenerRejectsImmediateWrapErrors` in this file.

`mustSendRecv` in `udp_test.go` and `mustSendRecvUDP` in `header/custom/state_test.go` use `t.Error`, which is safe from a goroutine, so they are unchanged.

### Verification

Forcing a write failure in the helper hangs the package for the full timeout before this change, and fails in 0.00s with the error after it. `go vet ./...` no longer reports the finding, and the package passes under `-race` and at `-count=30`.

issues.title: Observatory: fix data race in observation results
issues.body:
## Summary

Fix a data race in ordinary Observatory's `GetObservation` by returning an independent snapshot of the observation results.

## Problem

`GetObservation` currently returns a new `ObservationResult` containing references to the observer's internal status slice and messages.

Background probes update these statuses under `statusLock`, while consumers may read or serialize them after `GetObservation` returns.

This can cause concurrent reads and writes in routing strategies, metrics, and gRPC protobuf serialization.

The issue was reproduced on the current upstream `main` with Go's race detector, including a protobuf serialization error:

```text
WARNING: DATA RACE
size mismatch: calculated=22, measured=31
```

## Solution

Deep-clone the observation result while holding the existing `statusLock`:

```go
o.statusLock.Lock()
defer o.statusLock.Unlock()

return proto.Clone(&ObservationResult{Status: o.status}), nil
```

This ensures that callers receive an independent snapshot, including nested protobuf messages and unknown fields.

The existing synchronization mechanism, protobuf API, health checks, and routing behavior remain unchanged.

## Testing

Added two regression tests:

- **Snapshot isolation:** verifies that returned results do not share mutable state with the observer or other snapshots, including nested messages and unknown fields.
- **Concurrent access:** exercises status updates, additions, removals, and concurrent reads with protobuf serialization.

Both tests reproduce the original issue. The snapshot test also fails when using a mutex without deep copying.

Validation completed successfully:

- `go test -race ./app/observatory/...`
- `go test ./app/observatory/... ./app/router/... ./app/metrics/...`
- Xray build
- Formatting and diff checks

## Performance

Deep cloning introduces O(n) copying under the existing mutex. Benchmarks covering 2, 20, and 200 outbound statuses confirm the expected linear cost.

The fix intentionally favors correctness and minimal changes over additional synchronization complexity.

comments.issue_title: DNS outbound: End UDP sessions once their queries are answered
comments.body:
Reviewed head `d597417e` against base `f082058` — source, timer semantics, tests, CI. No blocking findings.

**The two commits since my earlier check fix what I reported.** `29eecf49` keys open queries by `{id, type, lower(name)}` with a count, so a duplicate answer to a settled query does nothing and can't drain the count while another query is still waiting — that's exactly the lost-answer case I reproduced with one socket, A answered twice, AAAA late. `d597417e` is not cosmetic either: `Periodic.Start()` runs `Execute()` immediately (`common/task/periodic.go`), so every `SetTimeout` consumes its own `Update` token. Without the extra `Update()` in `add()`, switching to the idle window burns the first period and an open query gets one `connIdle` instead of two. `done()` correctly does not need one — there the 1 s linger should start immediately.

**Checked beyond the commit messages:**

- The add/done pair lines up on both paths. `handleIPQuery` builds the synthetic answer with the client's `id` and question and writes it to the client directly, so the hijack path's `add`/`done` use the same key; `Direct` forwards the client's packet verbatim, so the upstream echo matches.
- Locking is sound: `add` and `done` both hold the mutex across the map mutation and the timer switch, so a new query cannot be followed by a stale switch to linger. Nil-receiver no-ops and the `overflow` latch (falling back to the idle timeout rather than half-tracking) both behave as documented.
- `answerTo` parses before `writer.WriteMessage` hands the buffer over — correct ordering, and the comment says why.

**Nits, not blockers:**

1. `TestUDPDNSSessionsEnd` asserts on `runtime.NumGoroutine()` with a `base + workers*perWorker/2` threshold and a 5 s deadline. That proves half the sessions went away, not that they went away for the right reason, and it is the kind of assertion that goes flaky on a loaded runner. Counting closed sessions through the dialer/stat path would be sharper.
2. An answer without a question section (`qdcount=0` REFUSED/NOTIMP — some stub resolvers and captive portals) settles nothing, so that session waits the full 2×`connIdle`, and each such answer logs a line through `parseQuery`'s `LogInfoInner`. Safe degradation; worth a sentence in the commit message rather than code.
3. A client that retransmits the same query on the same socket gets a count of 2 with one answer, so the session extends to the idle window. Already documented in the `pendingQueries` comment, so this is a note, not a defect.

Caveat on my side: reviewed from source plus the green CI on `d597417e`, not from a local test run — no Go toolchain here.

- [#3718](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/3718) and [#4988](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/4988): separate routing and sniffing state for each stream.
- [#6822](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/6822): the next UDP packet cannot overwrite the previous packet's address.
- [#4861](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/4861): check limits together with session allocation, and drain the remainder of a frame to its proper boundary after a child write failure.
- [#5288](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/5288): use the dispatcher interface without requiring a concrete `DefaultDispatcher`.
- [d20397c](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/d20397c15d59eff5e991423a9550fa9abc6eeefd) and [#5466](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/5466): user statistics with `DispatchLink`, without counting the whole Mux connection a second time.
- [#5110](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/5110) and [#4869](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/4869): Mux/Reverse termination and DRAIN handling while preserving active sessions.
- [#7359](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7359) and [#7375](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7375): interrupt a write without waiting for its lock, and retain the previous client concurrency settings: default 8, with a minimum of 128 only for XDrive.

In commit [37129ac](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7364/commits/37129aca050700baad51dd6db240dff87b1abd6e), I also fixed differences introduced by our migration:

- Restored XUDP retention across reconnection, introduced in [be23d5d](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/be23d5d3b741268ef86f27dfcb06389e97447e87). Closing the original inbound connection no longer terminates the retained outbound connection. Cancellation during opening and cancellation of ordinary sessions remain effective.
- Restored accounting before each delivery attempt, as in the [original `SizeStatWriter`](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/f082058590037e5c5363fd67017addbd2a3aecf3/app/dispatcher/stats.go). Rejected writes and retries are counted too. The first XUDP packet is still delivered before session registration.
- Restored GlobalID cleanup on initial dispatcher rejection from [76b27a3](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/76b27a37cb9d1f82baef901949d3fabc03fa63fa). The entry is removed before Mux closure becomes observable; late cleanup of the old connection cannot remove the new owner.

I also fixed a shutdown race in our implementation and a canceled reassociation that could destroy a healthy retained connection.

The earlier fixes are adapted to the new structure. I did not restore the old pipe-based implementation to preserve them.

Next I am working on:

1. Following [your naming comment](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7364#issuecomment-6842747639), make internal naming consistently use `Multiplex` and rename the Reverse sides to the internal-network side and the public-network side. Preserve external values required for compatibility.

3. Check a new client with an old server and an old client with a new server, including preservation of the fixes listed above after the transition.

comments.issue_title: proxy/tun: TUN fails to start on Windows 11 24H2 when DisabledComponents=0x28 ("unable to set DNS > Access is denied")
comments.body:
Thanks @patterniha for testing this and for the clear explanation. You were right: the problem was my Windows, not Xray.

**Root cause:** the registry key `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip6\Parameters` had broken permissions on my machine. It had apparently been deleted and recreated by some tool (owner `BUILTIN\Administrators` instead of `SYSTEM`, and the `Dhcpv6DUID` value and `Winsock` subkey were gone). The recreated key no longer had its own access rules, so it inherited the read-only rules of its parent `Tcpip6` key. As a result, `NETWORK SERVICE`, `NT SERVICE\Dhcp` and `Network Configuration Operators` had only read access there, while on `Tcpip\Parameters` (IPv4) they can write. Setting IPv6 DNS servers on the Wintun adapter writes under `Tcpip6\Parameters\Interfaces\{GUID}`, which is why `SetDNS(AF_INET6)` returned `Access is denied`. This also explains why the original v26.10.31 failed the same way.

**Fix:** I backed up the key, then copied the access rules (DACL) of `Tcpip\Parameters` onto `Tcpip6\Parameters`:

```powershell
$k6 = 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip6\Parameters'
$k4 = 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters'
(Get-Acl $k6).Sddl | Out-File tcpip6-acl-backup.txt
$acl = Get-Acl $k6
$acl.SetSecurityDescriptorSddlForm((Get-Acl $k4).GetSecurityDescriptorSddlForm('Access'), 'Access')
Set-Acl $k6 $acl
```

After that, the unmodified v26.11.9 started the TUN without errors, still with `DisabledComponents = 0x28`. Since I actually want IPv6 off, I then set `DisabledComponents = 0xFF` as you suggested and rebooted. Now IPv6 is gone from all interfaces, and v26.11.9 only logs `[tun] ignored, as DisabledComponents turns IPv6 off`, as documented.

If someone else hits `unable to set DNS > Access is denied` with a TUN config that only uses IPv4, compare the permissions of `Tcpip6\Parameters` with those of `Tcpip\Parameters` first.

Sorry for the noise, and thanks again for your time.

comments.issue_title: TLS: Fix data race between certificate hot reload and handshakes
comments.body:
I tested `d6abd207` on top of `main` at `c4561418` with Go 1.27.0 on Windows amd64.

- On clean `main`, the XHTTP TLS and QUIC tests both reported the certificate publication race. After applying this PR, that race was no longer reported in three runs of `go test -race -count=3 -run '^Test_ListenXHAndDial_(TLS|QUIC)$' ./transport/internet/splithttp`. The two certificate regression tests added here also passed five runs under `-race`.
- The only remaining race in that XHTTP rerun was the QUIC test's shared `serverClosed` Boolean. I opened #7391 for that test-only fix. With both patches applied locally, the XHTTP and HTTP Upgrade suites passed five runs under `-race`.

One remaining issue is ownership of the protobuf certificate. [`setupOcspTicker`](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/d6abd20773188970f2c63a5dd2ce8a75f618ac5e/transport/internet/tls/config.go#L103-L138) still assigns the reloaded PEM to `entry.Certificate` and `entry.Key`. `entry` is the same object held in `Config.Certificate`. I reproduced the mutation by creating a TLS config with an initial key pair in memory and a different valid pair at the configured paths. After `GetCertificate` returned the replacement, the original protobuf entry contained the replacement PEM too. That leaves a potential race with another `GetTLSConfig` call on the same config, since building the root pool also reads `entry.Certificate`.

Could the refresh goroutine keep its own copy of the protobuf certificate? My local prototype passes the reload check with both atomic publication and a goroutine-owned copy. In this PR, a small follow-up could clone the entry before starting the ticker and have the key-pair loader read the same copy.

comments.issue_title: VLESS: run multiplexing directly on transport
comments.body:
RPRX, I reworked Mux inside VLESS.

I removed the intermediate pipes from the VLESS Mux and Reverse paths. On the client, Mux passes data directly into the prepared VLESS connection. On the server, each stream is passed to the dispatcher through `DispatchLink` with its read and write endpoints already prepared. The existing VLESS codec, including Vision, is reused.

Changes by file:

- `multiplex/connection.go` and `vless/outbound/outbound.go`: direct access to the VLESS connection, decoded reads, error propagation, and connection shutdown.
- `multiplex/server.go` and the new `multiplex/xudp.go`: shared data handling for ordinary streams and XUDP. Data belongs to the flow, and the XUDP association survives reconnection. One emitter owns both data and stream completion.
- `multiplex/session.go`: removed duplicate server completion state. An old stream's completion cannot remove a newer binding with the same ID.
- Removed `multiplex/frame_sender.go`. Client sending now lives in `carrier.go`; server sending belongs to the flow emitter.
- In `carrier.go`, the sender combines **at most two already-ready batches**. It does not wait for another batch. Queue capacity and the four-frame encoding batch are unchanged.
- `client.go` and `reverse/portal.go`: updated connection opening and reuse, and Reverse control-message handling.
- `reader.go`: TCP data is still delivered as it arrives, while UDP packets remain whole. Data for a closed stream is drained to the end of its frame.
- `common/buf/writer.go`: added a way to invoke the existing write operation while its lock is already held. No additional lock is introduced.

Temporary storage for slow writes and UDP-association retention remains inside the flow handler.

Comparison with **original Xray at `f0820585`**:

- **One TCP stream, 512 MiB, and a parallel small latency probe, six rounds:** median throughput increased from **168.1 to 193.9 MiB/s**. Combined client/server CPU time for the same verified data volume decreased by about **5.3%**. Median loaded p95 latency was nearly unchanged. One run recorded a **307 ms** maximum latency.
- **Eight TCP streams, 1 GiB total, and a latency probe, six rounds:** throughput **253.3 → 332.0 MiB/s**, CPU time about **−6.1%**, and loaded p95 latency **28.8 → 21.3 ms**.
- **4 GiB upload:** I separately compared client sending with the same server for the two reworked-client cases. Combining ready batches improved throughput over the fixed final 2 GiB in all six paired runs, with a **3.95%** median increase. In this series, the new client was close to the original: **535.6 → 539.0 MiB/s**.
- **UDP through the real SOCKS → VLESS → server client path:** 100,000 packets at each of 64 and 1,200 bytes, with two opposite execution orders. Throughput was close to the original; combined CPU time for the two Xray processes was lower by about **2.6% and 7.3%**, respectively. Every packet and destination was validated. For 64-byte packets, individual maximum latencies were higher than the original.
- **Slow link:** transmission was byte-limited to 10 MiB/s in each direction. With 256 MiB of data, all variants completed and collected enough probe samples. Latency varied between rounds; no consistent benefit or penalty was established here.

The new commit changes **12 runtime Go files, +689/−450 lines against the previous PR head `05fc0e3f`**. Across the full PR, handwritten runtime Go code is **+2,226/−2,207 lines against the original, net +19**.

I am also considering removing the pipes from the VMess adapter.

`DisabledComponents = 0x28` doesn't disable IPv6: 0x08 only turns off Teredo, and 0x20 only makes Windows prefer IPv4. Only the 0x10 bit (as in 0x10, 0x11 or 0xFF) disables IPv6 on non-tunnel interfaces (the TUN, the primary adapter, ...).

I tested different modes on Windows 11 (build 26300), including `0x28`, each after a reboot, and IPv6 was set up successfully: `gateway`, `autoSystemRoutingTable` and `dns` were all applied. Your exact config with v26.11.9 and `0x28` also starts fine here, and the TUN's IPv6 DNS servers are cleared without errors. I only got errors with the 0x10 bit set, because only it disables IPv6 on the TUN interface.

So something is wrong with your Windows, and we shouldn't ignore IPv6 errors when IPv6 isn't disabled. If you want IPv6 off, set `DisabledComponents` to `0xFF` and reboot; then these IPv6 errors are only logged.

comments.issue_title: DNS outbound: End UDP sessions once their queries are answered
comments.body:
Ran this branch against a hand-rolled upstream on Windows to check the counter. The teardown itself checks out: copying the PR's `TestUDPDNSSessionsEnd` onto `main` reproduces the leak exactly (`sessions are still open: 604 goroutines above the baseline`), and it passes on the branch in 2.03s. A 2.5s lookup is also not cut (answered in 2.501s), so the linger doesn't trade away slow answers.

One finding though: the pending count isn't correlated with query identity, and that costs an answer when the upstream emits a second datagram for a single query. One client socket, A answered immediately, AAAA answered after 3s:

| upstream behaviour | main | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| one datagram per query | AAAA at 3.001s | AAAA at 3.002s |
| A answer repeated 300ms later | AAAA at 3.002s | AAAA never arrives (8s timeout) |

Mechanism: `add()` runs once per parsed query, `done()` once per message read from `connReader`. The duplicate takes the count 2 -> 1 -> 0 while the AAAA query is still outstanding, the session drops to the 1s linger, and the answer that lands at 3s has nowhere to go. On main there is no count, so the 300s idle window absorbed the extra datagram.

Triggers are anything that emits a second datagram for one query — a forwarder racing two upstreams and relaying both, a server resending on its own timeout, a reflected copy — and the exposure is exactly the A+AAAA pair from one stub socket, which is the case the linger exists to allow.

Keying pending queries by ID (a `map[uint16]` or a set, ignoring an `add()` for an ID already pending) and decrementing on the response's parsed ID would remove the class rather than this instance; it costs a header parse in `response()`. If it helps, the probe is a self-contained `proxy/dns` test that fails on the branch and passes on main — I can send it as a patch for the regression case.

### Describe the bug

On macOS, an XRay (VLESS + Reality) profile whose server address is a **domain name** never establishes: the app reaches "Connected", the `utun` interface is created but **never receives an IP address**, no traffic flows, and networking stays broken until disconnect. On disconnect the log shows `Failed to stop xray`.

Replacing only the server address with the server's **literal IPv4** (same key, same Reality parameters, same SNI) makes the very same profile work: `utun` gets its address and traffic flows.

### To Reproduce

1. Self-host xray-core (26.3.x), VLESS + Reality on TCP 443, with a DNS A record pointing at the server.
2. On macOS, import a `vpn://` key (or `vless://` link) where the outbound `vnext.address` is the **domain name**.
3. Connect. The app shows "Connected", but `ifconfig` shows the new `utun` interface without an inet address; nothing loads, the machine effectively loses networking until disconnect.
4. Re-import the same profile with `vnext.address` set to the server's literal IPv4 — it works: the `utun` gets its address (e.g. `10.x.x.x`) and traffic flows through the server.

### Expected behavior

A domain endpoint should work: resolve the name **before** the tunnel takes over the default route (or add a bypass route for the resolved IP once known). Otherwise the resolver query is routed into the tunnel that is still being established — a chicken-and-egg loop that can never complete.

### Evidence that it is the resolution order

- The same domain-based profile works in AmneziaVPN on **iOS**: the Network Extension excludes the provider's own traffic, so the name resolves outside the tunnel.
- The same domain-based `vless://` link works on the same Mac in a third-party client (V2Box), which resolves the name before route setup and adds a host bypass route for the resolved address.
- The "Use AmneziaDNS" toggle has no effect on this (tested both ways).
- Not a duplicate of #2722: there the tunnel comes up and passes IP traffic while in-tunnel DNS fails; here the tunnel never comes up at all when the address is a domain.

### Environment information

- **OS:** macOS 26 (Darwin 25.6)
- **AmneziaVPN Client Version:** 4.8.15.4 and 5.0.2.0 (both reproduce)
- **Protocol:** XRay, VLESS + Reality over TCP 443, self-hosted xray-core 26.3.x

Fixes #1607.

## Why a wildcard cannot simply be added to the list

Site split tunnelling selects by destination address, because that is all a
routing table has. The addresses behind `*.discord.gg` are not knowable when the
entry is typed, and a CDN keeps changing them, so there is nothing to install.
Entering a domain already works by resolving it once and storing the answer, but
a wildcard cannot be resolved at all: there is no query that returns every name
below a label.

The only place where the name still exists is the DNS exchange itself. This
change puts a forwarder where the system already sends its queries, relays them
to the real resolvers, and installs an exclusion route for the addresses of the
answers whose name matches a pattern, while the answer is still on its way back
to the application.

## What is in it

Four commits, each one reviewable on its own:

1. **The forwarder, the shared definition of a wildcard, and the route table.**
   No caller yet.
2. **The UI and configuration path**: storing a pattern, and carrying it to the
   daemon.
3. **The daemon and the platform work**: installing, permitting and withdrawing
   what is learned.
4. **Fixes from the review** below: reserved addresses, the server switch, route
   lifetime, per-pattern budgets, dedicated firewall anchors on Linux and macOS,
   UDP/TCP failover in the forwarder, client-side gating and log privacy.

### Trusting an answer

What the forwarder reports becomes a route in a privileged daemon, so a reply is
believed only when all of this holds: it arrived from the resolver the query was
sent to, on a socket connected to it; the transaction id and the question match
the query; the response bit is set, the opcode is zero, there is no error, and
the answer is not truncated. Addresses are taken only from records whose owner is
the queried name or a name reached from it through the CNAMEs of that same
message, and each address inherits the shortest TTL along that path. Everything
else is handed to the application untouched and reported to nobody.

Because the forwarder replaces the system's resolver list, it does the
failover the system would otherwise do. A UDP query is retransmitted across
the configured resolvers (1 s per attempt, 5 s in total, a single resolver
being retried), a late answer to an earlier attempt is still accepted, and the
resolver that answered last is tried first. A TCP resolver that closes with
queries outstanding is reconnected and the queries resent. Only when the budget
runs out is the query answered with SERVFAIL, rather than left to time out.

Queries are served from the machine itself and from directly attached
subnets of other interfaces (local containers). Peers reaching the address
over the tunnel are refused, because what the forwarder learns becomes a
route.

### Names are never flattened

A DNS label may legally contain a dot. Names coming off the wire are kept as a
list of labels and compared label by label, so a single label whose bytes read
`x.example.com` does not pass for a name below `example.com`. Patterns are stored
canonically: lower case, no trailing dot, the base put through IDNA, and a path,
white space or an empty label refused at the point of entry. `*.пример.рф` is
stored as `*.xn--e1afmkfd.xn--p1ai`, which is the form that actually arrives.

### How long a learned route lives

A learned route lasts for the session. It is not withdrawn on a timer: an open
connection keeps using the address after the TTL, and the system resolver can
serve the record from its cache for as long as the TTL says. Once the full TTL
plus an hour has passed (on a monotonic clock), the entry is stale. A stale
entry is evicted, least recently seen first, only when its pattern or the
table is full. All learned routes are withdrawn on disconnect, on a server
switch to a different configuration, and when the pattern list changes.

issues.title: WG/AWG .conf import silently ignores a single DNS server and uses application DNS
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

Importing a valid WireGuard `.conf` file with exactly one IPv4 DNS server silently discards that DNS setting. On Android, the resulting VPN network receives the application's DNS values instead of the server specified in the file.

The connection itself succeeds, so this is easy to miss when public names still resolve. It breaks resolution of private names available only through the configured resolver.

**Environment**

- AmneziaVPN: 5.0.3.0
- Client OS: Android 16
- Protocol tested: ordinary WireGuard, without AmneziaWG obfuscation
- Profile imported from a `.conf` file

**To Reproduce**

1. Take a working WireGuard configuration and specify a single reachable IPv4 DNS server in `[Interface]`, for example:
   ```ini
   DNS = 10.23.0.53
   ```
   This is an illustrative private address, not an address from the tested setup.
2. Leave the application DNS settings at their defaults (`1.1.1.1` and `1.0.0.1`).
3. Import the file as a new profile and connect.
4. Inspect the active VPN network's `DnsAddresses` in `adb shell dumpsys connectivity`.

**Actual behavior**

The configured private resolver is absent. The captured VPN network state contained:

```text
InterfaceName: tun0
DnsAddresses: [ /1.1.1.1,/1.0.0.1 ]
```

The intended private DNS server was independently tested from the phone: a direct UDP/53 DNS query returned a successful response. This is a DNS configuration/import problem, rather than evidence that the intended resolver is unreachable.

Android Private DNS was in automatic (`opportunistic`) mode during the captured baseline. The incorrect addresses were already present in the VPN's `DnsAddresses`; this report concerns which servers the VPN registers with Android, not a DNS leak-test website's result.

**Expected behavior**

A valid single DNS address in an imported WireGuard configuration should be retained and applied to the VPN network. It should not silently disappear because no second DNS address is provided.

**Source-level cause**

In tag `5.0.3.0`, `ImportController::extractWireGuardConfig()` uses a DNS regular expression with two mandatory IPv4 capture groups. It only populates the profile's `dns1` and `dns2` when that entire expression matches:

https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/5.0.3.0/client/core/controllers/selfhosted/importController.cpp#L645-L652

Consequently:

- `DNS = 10.23.0.53` does not match.
- `DNS = 10.23.0.53, 10.23.0.54` matches.

When profile DNS fields are absent, `NativeServerConfig::getDnsPair()` falls back to the application settings:

https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/5.0.3.0/client/core/models/selfhosted/nativeServerConfig.cpp#L38-L49

The application defaults are `1.1.1.1` and `1.0.0.1`:

https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/5.0.3.0/client/core/repositories/secureAppSettingsRepository.cpp#L74-L88

The same import function handles both WireGuard and AmneziaWG profiles. The device-level reproduction above used ordinary WireGuard.

**Workaround**

Add a second reachable private DNS server to the same line and import the modified file as a new profile:

```ini
DNS = 10.23.0.53, 10.23.0.54
```

After this change, the previously failing name resolution in Chrome started working in the tested setup.

**Suggested fix**

Parse the DNS field as a list and preserve a valid single entry. Add regression coverage for a single IPv4 DNS address and two comma-separated IPv4 addresses, including verification that the single-entry case does not silently fall back to the application primary DNS.

**Related issues**

- #2957 concerns imported profile DNS taking precedence over application settings. This report concerns a valid single DNS entry being lost during import.
- #3059 reports ignored DNS settings on Android, without identifying this single-entry parsing failure.

issues.title: Stuck in infinite "Reconnecting..." loop when disconnecting OpenVPN over Cloak on Windows 11
issues.body:
Describe the bug
When using AmneziaVPN (version 4.8.19.0) on Windows 11 with the OpenVPN over Cloak protocol, the application fails to terminate the connection properly. Clicking the "Disconnect" button triggers an infinite "Reconnecting..." state in the UI. The only way to stop it is to kill the process via Task Manager.

To Reproduce

Select a server with OpenVPN over Cloak protocol.
Click Connect and wait for a successful connection.
Click Disconnect.
The status changes to "Reconnecting..." and stays in this state indefinitely.
Expected behavior
The connection should terminate immediately, and the UI should return to the "Disconnected" state.

Logs & Technical Details
Based on preliminary observation, the issue seems to be a race condition/state conflict between the Cloak transport and the OpenVPN client:

Upon manual disconnection, the OpenVPN instance appears to receive a connection-reset or similar signal from the Cloak layer.
Instead of interpreting the disconnect as a "Stop" command, the OpenVPN client treats it as an accidental drop and triggers a SIGUSR1 (soft restart).
The Amnezia GUI becomes stuck waiting for the process to exit, while the process is trying to re-establish the tunnel.
Environment:

AmneziaVPN Version: 4.8.19.0
OS: Windows 11
Protocol: OpenVPN over Cloak
Installation method: Standard Windows Installer (installed via Amnezia client).
Possible Workarounds/Fixes suggested:

Adding remap-usr1 SIGTERM to the OpenVPN client configuration to force exit on resets.
Implementing explicit-exit-notify 1 (for UDP) or adjusting keepalive / ping-restart timers to be less aggressive during the shutdown phase.
Ensuring the GUI sends a hard SIGTERM or taskkill equivalent to the OpenVPN process when the user clicks "Disconnect".

issues.body:
FIX importat IOS network extension break down.
On iOS the network extension was jetsam-killed at the 50 MB limit a few minutes
after connecting to an xhttp + REALITY server (`The VPN plugin died unexpectedly`).

With `mode` unset xray picks `stream-one` for xhttp + REALITY: one endless POST
per session, and Go's HTTP/2 client holds a 512 KiB scratch buffer per such
stream for its whole lifetime. A heap profile from the extension showed
`http2.(*clientStream).writeRequestBody` at 34.5 MB (74 % of the Go heap) with
~70 sessions, which Instagram/Facebook open within a minute.

The extension now sets `xhttpSettings.mode = "packet-up"` when the mode is empty
or `auto`: each POST has a `Content-Length`, so the buffer is payload-sized and
transient. An explicit mode is left as is; the server accepts both modes.
iOS extension only.

comments.body:
Thanks for the careful review and the question. You were right on every point, including the Docker one, which I confirmed in the code. The fixes are in d5eb7302. Per point:

## Scope: "Via VPN" mode

No, this PR covers only the "Directly" (bypass) mode. In "Via VPN" mode a wildcard is refused at entry with an explanation, and an imported one is skipped and reported. The reason is how it works: the daemon learns addresses from the DNS answers that pass through the forwarder and installs exclusion routes for them. The opposite mode needs include routes into a tunnel that is not the default route, with the forwarder's own upstream traffic routed accordingly. That is a different change, and I would rather do it as a follow-up than grow this one.

What this PR does support:
- **Platforms:** the desktop daemon only (Windows, Linux, macOS non-NE). Android, iOS and the macOS network extension refuse the entry with a message.
- **Protocols:** WireGuard / AmneziaWG only. The site list is shared across servers, so on desktop the entry stays in the list. With an OpenVPN or XRay server it is left out of the connection config, so it no longer keeps the route mode at "split" with an empty list. The UI says the entry applies to WireGuard/AmneziaWG connections.
- **IPv6:** on Linux, learned AAAA addresses stay in the tunnel, because the route monitor builds IPv4 exclusion routes only.
- **Testing:** only Windows has been built and tested. Linux and macOS have been reviewed but not compiled.

## Review findings

1. **Reserved addresses (`daemon.cpp:268`).** The reserved list now also covers the forwarder's upstream resolvers, the other allowed DNS servers, both gateways, both server addresses, and the tunnel's own network. An explicit prefix on the device address is taken as given, /32 included. A bare private (or ULA/CGNAT) address reserves its /24 (/64). A bare public address is reserved as a host only. So an answer containing 1.1.1.1, AmneziaDNS or the peer can no longer route DNS or in-tunnel services out of the tunnel.
2. **`switchServer` and the macOS DNS backup (`daemon.cpp:765`).** The `maybeUpdateResolvers` call in `switchServer` is removed. `activate()` already does restore-then-update right after it returns, so the original backup is kept again.
3. **TTL-bound expiry (`daemon.cpp:337`).** Learned routes are no longer withdrawn on a timer, and the TTL is no longer clamped. A route lives for the session. Once the full TTL plus an hour of grace has passed, the entry becomes stale, and a stale entry is evicted only when its pattern (or the table) is full; until then it is never withdrawn. A day-long record therefore keeps its route at least for the day the OS may serve it from cache. One limitation remains, and I'd rather state it than hide it: if a pattern is full, a connection that has stayed open for over an hour past the TTL, with no new lookup of that name, can lose its bypass route when a new address is learned. Not evicting at all would trade that for new subdomains silently going through the VPN once a pattern is full, which seemed the worse default.
4. **Linux firewall cost and stale snapshot (`wireguardutilslinux.cpp:552`, `:535`).** Wildcard permits now live in their own anchor, `240.allowWildcard`, IPv4 and IPv6 alike. It sits ahead of `250.blockIPv6`/`100.blockAll`, and nothing else writes to it, so `KillSwitch::resetAllowedRange` can no longer wipe it. A new address costs a single idempotent `iptables -C || -A`, and a disconnect costs one flush. The `FirewallParams` snapshot is gone. The active flag is reset on `addInterface`/`deleteInterface`, and when the firewall turns out to be removed it is not written to. A peer update within a session (server switch) no longer clears the anchor, and the daemon re-asserts the retained permits when it keeps the observer. macOS gets the same treatment: anchor `320.allowWildcard`, placed after `310.blockDNS`, with its own tables and one `pfctl -T add/delete` per address.

comments.body:
# [SOLVED] AmneziaVPN Error 305/302 on Ubuntu 24.04 VPS — SSH socket listening on IPv6 only

I'd like to share a solution to an issue that prevented me from adding my self-hosted VPN server to AmneziaVPN on Windows.

**Environment:**
- VPS provider: Fornex
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- VPN client: AmneziaVPN for Windows
- VPN protocol: AmneziaWG 2.0
- ISP: Dom.ru (Russia)
- A MacBook on the same office network could still connect to the existing VPN, while the Windows client could not add the server.

**Symptoms:**

When adding the VPS to AmneziaVPN via SSH, the Windows client returned:

`ErrorCode: 305 — Timeout connecting to server`

When I routed the connection through another working VPN, the error changed to:

`ErrorCode: 302 — SSH Internal Error`

Diagnostics showed:
- The VPS responded to ping and traceroute completed successfully.
- The SSH service was running.
- SSH appeared to listen on TCP ports 22 and 443.
- UFW was inactive, the iptables INPUT policy was ACCEPT, and the hosting provider's firewall was disabled.
- Direct TCP connections to ports 22 and 443 failed from Windows.
- Through another VPN, TCP/22 became reachable, but OpenSSH failed before authentication:

```text
ssh_exchange_identification: Connection closed by remote host
```

- A local IPv4 connection test from the VPS to `127.0.0.1:22` returned `Connection refused`.

**Root cause identified:**

The Ubuntu `ssh.socket` configuration included:

```ini
BindIPv6Only=ipv6-only
```

Meanwhile, `/etc/systemd/system/ssh.socket.d/override.conf` contained:

```ini
[Socket]
ListenStream=
ListenStream=22
ListenStream=443
```

As a result, SSH was listening on IPv6 sockets (`[::]:22` and `[::]:443`), while IPv4 connections were not being accepted.

**Fix:**

I updated `/etc/systemd/system/ssh.socket.d/override.conf` to explicitly bind both IPv4 and IPv6:

```ini
[Socket]
ListenStream=
ListenStream=0.0.0.0:22
ListenStream=[::]:22
ListenStream=0.0.0.0:443
ListenStream=[::]:443
```

Then applied the configuration:

```bash
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart ssh.socket
```

Verification:

```bash
ss -4 -tlnp
```

The output now showed `0.0.0.0:22` and `0.0.0.0:443` listening.

**Result:**

With a temporary VPN connection (Happ), I was able to add the VPS to AmneziaVPN successfully.

I then completely disabled Happ and connected through AmneziaWG directly over my office ISP connection.

IPinfo showed the VPS public IP, and internet access worked normally.

The existing AmneziaWG 2.0 installation was left untouched, and the previously configured MacBook connection continued working.

**Important notes:**

- A working VPN tunnel on one device does not necessarily imply that SSH access is available for adding the same server on another device.
- `sshd` being active and showing `[::]:22` does not guarantee IPv4 connectivity.
- The fix applies to this particular `ssh.socket` configuration. Check your actual socket settings before changing them.
- The initial direct TCP connectivity failures were not independently attributed to the ISP. Therefore, I cannot conclusively claim that IPv4 socket configuration was the sole cause of every observed connection failure.

**References:**

- Ubuntu Launchpad Bug #2080216: https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/openssh/+bug/2080216
- Related AmneziaVPN Error 305 discussion: https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/issues/1624

Hopefully this helps others experiencing AmneziaVPN SSH errors 305/302 on Ubuntu 24.04. #
